CC 2. Approve the Check and Wire Registers for April 30, 2017 â€“ May 20, 2017 in the amount of $5,738,061.79. Approve the Check Registers as presented.
At each regular City Council Meeting, the City Council is presented with the financial claims (invoices) against the City for purchase of materials, supplies, services, and capital projects for checks and Automated Clearing House (ACH) payments issued the prior two to three weeks. This process provides the City Council the opportunity to review the expenses of the City. The justifying backup information for each expenditure is available in the Finance Department.

CC 3. Adopt Ordinance 1022, amending Chapter 17.08 of the Lancaster Municipal Code to establish regulations for the grazing of animals in the RR-2.5 and RR-1 Zones.
This ordinance prohibits â€œfree-rangeâ€ grazing, requiring that all grazing animals be controlled to prevent them from straying onto adjacent property. Grazing is only permitted to occur on property owned by the owner of the animals, or on property in which the herder has the written permission of the property owner. The owner of the animals is responsible for managing the grazing activity to prevent excessive removal of vegetation, and both the owner of the animals and the property owner are responsible for implementing any dust control measures in compliance with the City code and the requirements of the Antelope Valley Air Quality Management District (AVAQMD).

NB 2. Amendments to the Lancaster Municipal Code relating to the Criminal Justice Commission, the Architectural and Design Commission, the Neighborhood Vitalization Commission and creating two new Commissions
Recommendations:
NB 2
NB 2 attachment
a.
Introduce Ordinance No. 1024, amending Chapter 2.30 of the Lancaster Municipal Code to change the procedure for setting the time and date for meetings held by the Criminal Justice Commission as well as other changes.
b.
Introduce Ordinance No. 1025, amending Chapter 2.34 of the Lancaster Municipal Code regarding the Architectural and Design Planning Commission.
c.
Introduce Ordinance No. 1026, adding Chapter 2.37 to the Lancaster Municipal Code creating the Lancaster Homeless Impact Commission.
d.
Introduce Ordinance No. 1027, amending Chapter 2.38 of the Lancaster Municipal Code abolishing the Neighborhood Vitalization Commission and creating the Lancaster Healthy Community Commission.
The City of Lancaster has several Commissions that serve in an advisory capacity to the City Council. Commissioners are residents of, or primarily employed in, the City of Lancaster and the Antelope Valley and appointed by the Mayor with consent of the Council. Members of City Commissions serve an important role to help shape the policies under which the City operates. Commissioners provide a vital link between residents, City Council, and City staff to ensure our local government remains dynamic, responsive and accountable. At the May 23, 2017, City Council meeting, Mayor Parris presented to Council the discussion of City Commissions, specifically the establishment of two new Commissions, and directed staff to present an item to the City Council identifying the necessary course of action.
NB 3. Adoption of City-wide Safe Routes to School Master Plan
Recommendation:
Adopt Resolution No. 17-27, approving the City of Lancaster Safe Routes to School Master Plan.
NB 3
NB 3 attachment
The Safe Routes to School (SRTS) Master Plan was initiated by the City of Lancaster in 2013, and was funded by two different grants, a Healthy Eating Active Living (HEAL) grant through the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, and an Active Transportation Program (ATP) grant through the State of California. The plan builds on the efforts of the City's adopted Master Plan of Trails and Bikeways by further identifying improvements and programs that can make the neighborhoods around the schools safer for pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists. The plan will help direct, and will assist the City in obtaining, grant funding for improvements, such as sidewalks, bike facilities, and installation of traffic calming devices.
NB 4. Introduction of Ordinance to Establish Speed Limits and Amend Section 10.04.020 of the Lancaster Municipal Code
Recommendation:
Introduce Ordinance No. 1023, establishing speed limits in the City of Lancaster based on the Engineering and Traffic Survey Report dated March 2017 prepared by Albert Grover and Associates, and Addendum dated May 2017, and amend Section 10.04.020, Subparagraph D of the Lancaster Municipal Code.
The purpose of the proposed ordinance is to adopt the speed limits on the City of Lancaster arterial and collector street network determined by the Engineering and Traffic Survey dated March 2017 and the Addendum dated May 2017. The studies were conducted to comply with existing state regulations concerning the increasing or decreasing of speed limits within City boundaries.

PUBLIC HEARINGS
PH 1. Proposed Fiscal Year 2017-2018 Budget and Five-Year Capital Improvement Program
Recommendation:
City Council and City Council acting as Lancaster Housing Authority, Lancaster Choice Energy, Lancaster Power Authority, and California Choice Energy Authority conduct the public hearing on the Proposed Fiscal Year 2017-2018 Budget and Five-Year Capital Improvement Plan, and schedule the budget for adoption on June 27, 2017.
PH 1
The Proposed FY 2017-2018 Budget is balanced, with healthy General Fund Reserves that will enable the City to continue to provide the community with a full scope of high quality municipal services, programs and special events that enhance the quality of life of all Lancaster residents. It will also provide the required resources to construct significant capital improvement projects that will improve infrastructure and facilities, and beautify the community.
PH 2. Lancaster Lighting Maintenance District for Fiscal Year 2017-2018
Recommendation:
Adopt Resolution No. 17-28, confirming the diagram and assessment and ordering the levying of an assessment in Lancaster Lighting Maintenance District for Fiscal Year 2017-2018.
PH 2
PH 2 attachment
Lancaster Lighting Maintenance District was formed, including subsequent annexations thereto, for the purpose of financing maintenance operations and installation of public lighting facilities, including, but not limited to, traffic signals (as defined in Â§ 22525 of the California Code) within the City of Lancaster, and assessing those properties which benefit from this service their proportionate share of the cost. Each year, the City Council must, by law, order the preparation of an Engineer's Report describing the existing and proposed maintenance services, and conduct a public hearing to establish and order the amount of assessment for the next fiscal year.
PH 3. Lancaster Landscape Maintenance District No. 1 for Fiscal Year 2017-2018
Recommendation:
Adopt Resolution No. 17-29, confirming the diagram and assessment and ordering the levying of an assessment in Lancaster Landscape Maintenance District No. 1 for Fiscal Year 2017-2018.
PH 3
PH 3 attachment
Lancaster Landscape Maintenance District No. 1 and Fox Field Industrial Corridor Landscape Maintenance District were formed, including subsequent annexations thereto, for the purpose of providing maintenance services to landscaping and appurtenant improvements for various developments within the City and assessing those properties which benefit from this service. Each year, the City Council must, by law, order the preparation of an Engineer's Report describing the existing and proposed maintenance services, and conduct a public hearing to establish and order the amount of assessment for the next fiscal year.
PH 4. Lancaster Drainage Benefit Assessment District Levy of Annual Assessment for Fiscal Year 2017-2018
Recommendation:
Adopt Resolution No. 17-30, confirming the diagram and assessment, and ordering the levying of an assessment in Lancaster Drainage Benefit Assessment District for Fiscal Year 2017-2018.
PH 4
PH 4 attachment
The City Council previously formed the Lancaster Drainage Benefit Assessment District, including establishment of separate zones, and submitted the proposition to the eligible voters in each respective zone. The majority of voters approved the formation of the District, the separate zones, and the levying of the assessment. The first year's assessment was paid by the developers of the property. Each year, thereafter, the City Council, after public notice and hearing, may determine and impose an annual assessment.
